hypothesis: Stature-velocity curves for ages 8 to 19 are nearly the same shape in boys and girls, but the girls' adolescent acceleration starts, peaks and ends earlier than the boys', and the two sexes differ in peak amplitude.
pass_criterion: All of the following hold, using survey-weighted NHANES mean stature at exact age in months (RIDAGEEX), smoothed with a spline, differentiated to cm/yr, and pooled over cycles with MEC exam weights. (1) Shape similarity: the Pearson r between the girls' and boys' velocity curves over ages 8 to 19, after shifting the boys' curve by the best-fitting lag, is at least 0.90. (2) Phase: the age at peak height velocity is earlier in girls than in boys by at least 1.0 year, with the 95% bootstrap CI of the difference excluding 0. (3) Onset and end: the age at which velocity rises above its pre-pubertal minimum plus 1 cm/yr, and the age at which it falls back below 2 cm/yr after the peak, are both earlier in girls, each with a bootstrap CI excluding 0. (4) Amplitude: peak velocities differ between the sexes by at least 0.5 cm/yr, with a bootstrap CI excluding 0.
fail_criterion: The claim is refuted if any of these holds. (a) The lag-aligned shape correlation is below 0.80. (b) The girls' peak-velocity age is not earlier than the boys' by at least 0.5 year, or the bootstrap CI includes 0. (c) Either the onset or the end of the acceleration is not earlier in girls. (d) The peak velocities differ by less than 0.5 cm/yr, or the bootstrap CI includes 0. Results between the pass and fail thresholds are reported as inconclusive.
interpretation: Thompson's 'curve of growth velocity' is the first derivative of stature with respect to age, in cm/yr. 'Phase' is the horizontal timing shift of the adolescent acceleration: its onset, its peak (PHV age) and its end. 'Amplitude' is the peak height velocity. Thompson drew on longitudinal data (Quetelet, Bowditch and others), whereas NHANES is a repeated cross-section. Velocity is therefore estimated from the derivative of the smoothed weighted mean-stature-by-age curve, not from individual increments. This blurs and slightly delays the peak, because individuals mature at different times, but it affects both sexes in the same way. This is a modern reinterpretation. Only measured stature (BMXHT) is used, and only ages 2 to 19.

dataset.name: National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) – Body Measures (BMX) and Demographics (DEMO)
dataset.publisher: US CDC National Center for Health Statistics
dataset.why_it_fits: NHANES records measured standing height (BMXHT, cm) in the Body Measures files. The Demographics files hold sex (RIAGENDR), age in months at exam (RIDAGEEX), age in years (RIDAGEYR) and the MEC exam weight (WTMEC2YR). Both files can be downloaded as SAS transport files and joined on SEQN across cycles. The survey covers ages 2 to 19 in both sexes, enough to estimate sex-specific velocity curves and bootstrap their features.
